outline.description: This chapter introduces the factual background of the case, including the parties, Consilio's overtime policy change, and Cohen's lawsuit alleging violations of three Minnesota wage statutes. It covers the procedural developments leading to summary judgment, including Consilio's payment of overtime wages and liquidated damages, the parties' stipulations, and the agreed-upon path to resolve the case through summary judgment. The chapter also explains the standard of review for summary judgment on appeal.
subtopics: The parties: Consilio as a nationwide legal document review company and Cohen as an hourly licensed attorney document reviewer in Minnesota
Consilio's July 2019 email instituting a new premium overtime policy eliminating overtime premium pay
Cohen's August 2020 lawsuit on behalf of himself and a putative class alleging violations of the MPWA, MFLSA, and MWTA
Remedies sought: overtime pay, liquidated damages, statutory penalties, and injunctive relief
Consilio's payment of $256,010.01 to cover overtime wages and liquidated damages under the MFLSA, with Cohen personally receiving $3,225.21 in overtime and $462 in liquidated damages
The parties' stipulation that Cohen had been paid all overtime wages and liquidated damages he alleges he is owed
The dispute over penalties: Cohen's demand for $172,080 under MPWA, $42,000 under MFLSA, and $42,000 under MWTA; Consilio's position that the statutes do not permit Cohen to obtain penalties
The parties' agreement to resolve the case through summary judgment before further discovery or litigation
The district court's grant of summary judgment to Consilio on all three claims and Cohen's appeal
Standard of review: de novo review of summary judgment, viewing evidence in the light most favorable to the nonmoving party

outline.chapter_title: The MPWA Claim: Statutory Interpretation and the Commissioner's Exclusive Role in Seeking Penalties
outline.description: This chapter examines the court's analysis of Cohen's claim under the Minnesota Payment of Wages Act (MPWA). The court interprets §§ 181.171 and 181.101 to determine whether an employee can seek 'average daily wage penalties' or whether that authority is reserved exclusively to the Commissioner. The chapter explains the court's use of statutory interpretation principles, including plain language analysis and comparison to other Minnesota statutes, to conclude that only the Commissioner may seek such penalties.
subtopics: The statutory framework: § 181.171 as the enforcement mechanism for certain MPWA provisions including § 181.101
§ 181.171's provision that an employer found to have violated the MPWA is liable for 'civil penalties or damages provided for in the section violated'
Cohen's argument that the plain language of § 181.101 authorizes employees to seek average daily wage penalties
The court's plain language analysis of § 181.101(a): penalties are referenced only in connection with the Commissioner
The procedural prerequisites for penalties under § 181.101(a): the Commissioner must first serve a demand for payment, and only then may charge and collect wages and a penalty
The statutory directive that money collected by the Commissioner must be paid to the employee
The employee's reserved right under § 181.101(a) to 'prosecute a claim for wages' — distinguished from seeking penalties

The court's comparison to other Minnesota statutes (§ 181.13(a) for discharged employees, § 181.14 subd. 2 for employees who quit) where the legislature expressly empowered employees to collect penalties
The legislative inference: the legislature 'knows how' to empower employees to seek penalties and chose not to do so under § 181.101
The court's holding: only the Commissioner may seek daily average wage penalties under § 181.101; affirmance of summary judgment

outline.chapter_title: The MFLSA Claim: Standing, Mootness, and the Jurisdictional Question of Civil Penalties Payable to the Government
outline.description: This chapter analyzes the court's treatment of Cohen's MFLSA claim for statutory penalties after he stipulated to receiving all overtime wages and liquidated damages. The court raised a serious jurisdictional concern regarding whether Cohen has standing to seek civil penalties payable to the Commissioner rather than to himself. The chapter explains the standing and mootness doctrines as applied to civil penalties, the voluntary cessation doctrine, and the court's decision to vacate and remand for a jurisdictional determination. It also covers Judge Kobes's special concurrence questioning whether standing exists under the Friends of the Earth framework.
subtopics: Cohen's stipulation that Consilio compensated him for all overtime wages and liquidated damages under the MFLSA
Cohen's remaining claim for statutory penalties under the MFLSA, with the parties agreeing such penalties are payable to the Commissioner, not to Cohen
The court's sua sponte concern regarding jurisdiction to decide the MFLSA penalty issue
Standing requirements: a plaintiff must demonstrate standing for each claim and each form of relief sought (Town of Chester v. Laroe Estates)
The relationship between standing and mootness: the requisite personal interest at the commencement of litigation must continue throughout its existence (Sisney v. Kaemingk)
Friends of the Earth v. Laidlaw: civil penalties payable to the government may afford redress to citizen plaintiffs by encouraging discontinuation of violations and deterring future ones
Mootness doctrine: a claim may become moot if subsequent events make it absolutely clear that the wrongful behavior could not reasonably be expected to recur
The voluntary cessation doctrine: a defendant's voluntary cessation of a challenged practice does not automatically deprive a federal court of jurisdiction
The disputed factual question of whether Consilio's violative overtime policy remains in place
The court's disposition: vacatur of summary judgment on the MFLSA claim and remand for the district court to determine its jurisdiction

Judge Kobes's special concurrence: skepticism about Cohen's standing under Friends of the Earth due to differences between penalties in that case and MFLSA penalties; agreement that the claim might be moot; recommendation that the district court decide the mootness question first on remand

outline.chapter_title: The MWTA Claim and Injunctive Relief: Procedural Default and the Failure to Properly Raise Claims
outline.description: This chapter addresses the remaining two claims: Cohen's MWTA claim alleging failure to provide statutorily required notice of the overtime policy change, and his claim for injunctive relief. The court affirmed dismissal of the MWTA claim due to Cohen's failure to point to any statutory authority for civil penalties and lack of meaningful argument. The injunctive relief claim was not properly before the court because Cohen changed the specific relief sought between his complaint and summary judgment briefing without amending his complaint. The chapter explains the procedural principles underlying both affirmances.
subtopics: Cohen's MWTA claim: alleged failure by Consilio to provide statutorily required notice of a change in its overtime policy under § 181.032(f), (d)(4)
Cohen's complaint that the district court included little to no discussion of this claim
The effect of Cohen's stipulation that he received all pay Consilio owes him on the MWTA claim
Cohen's failure to point to any statutory authority allowing for civil penalties under the MWTA
The court's application of the waiver principle: failure to support an assertion with argument or legal authority constitutes waiver (Milligan v. City of Red Oak)
Affirmance of dismissal of the MWTA claim
Cohen's claim for injunctive relief: request for an affirmative order that Consilio rescind its illegal overtime policy
The discrepancy between the specific injunctive relief sought in Cohen's complaint and the different relief requested in his summary judgment briefing
The district court's understandable failure to consider the new form of injunctive relief
The procedural rule: new claims must be raised through amended complaints, not opposition briefs (InfoDeli, LLC; Fed. R. Civ. P. 15(a))
The court's conclusion that the injunctive relief issue is not properly before it
